# What a modeller does during an outbreak

## The loop

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Counts arrive by report date. The infections happened days or weeks
  earlier
- Estimate the delays first, then unpick them from the counts to get
  infections and $R_t$
- A renewal process. Today's infections are $R_t$ times a weighted sum
  of recent infections
- Someone decides. Then next week's data arrive
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-loop.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Four teal boxes in a row, data arrive, delays, infections and
Rt, forecasts and scenarios, joined by arrows, with a red box labelled a
decision below and a red return arrow labelled new data, next week
running back to the first box."}

::: {.attribution}
Diagram this talk, `scripts/keynote-schematics.py`, after
[A workflow for infectious disease modelling][wf], Abbott et al.
:::
:::

## A renewal process, by hand

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- $I_t = R_t \sum_s I_{t-s}\, g_s$
- $g_s$ is the generation interval (GI), the delay from one infection
  to the next
- Above one, growth. Below one, decline. The generation interval sets
  how fast
- Move the sliders
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
<style>
.reveal .slides form[class^="oi-"] {
  --label-width: 260px; --input-width: 460px;
}
</style>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof R = Inputs.range([0.5, 1.8], {
  value: 1.3, step: 0.05, label: "R"
})
viewof gmean = Inputs.range([2, 12], {
  value: 5, step: 0.5, label: "Mean GI, days"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
renewal = {
  const days = 60, k = 4, theta = gmean / k, support = 24;
  const g = Array.from({length: support}, (_, i) => {
    const s = i + 1;
    return Math.pow(s, k - 1) * Math.exp(-s / theta);
  });
  const gsum = g.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const gn = g.map((v) => v / gsum);
  // Growth rate from the Euler-Lotka equation, R * sum g_s exp(-r s) = 1,
  // by bisection. Seeding on that exponential, ten on day 0, keeps the
  // series a straight line on the log scale from the first day.
  let lo = -2, hi = 2;
  for (let i = 0; i < 80; i++) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    const f = R * gn.reduce((a, v, j) => a + v * Math.exp(-mid * (j + 1)), 0);
    if (f > 1) lo = mid; else hi = mid;
  }
  const rate = (lo + hi) / 2;
  const inf = new Array(support + days).fill(0);
  for (let t = 0; t < support; t++) {
    inf[t] = 10 * Math.exp(rate * (t - support + 1));
  }
  for (let t = support; t < inf.length; t++) {
    let s = 0;
    for (let j = 0; j < support; j++) s += inf[t - 1 - j] * gn[j];
    inf[t] = R * s;
  }
  return inf.slice(support - 1).map((y, t) => ({day: t, infections: y}));
}
logTicks = {
  const ys = renewal.map((d) => d.infections);
  const lo = Math.floor(Math.log10(Math.min(...ys) / 1.5));
  const hi = Math.ceil(Math.log10(Math.max(...ys) * 1.5));
  return Array.from({length: hi - lo + 1}, (_, i) => Math.pow(10, lo + i));
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 1000,
  height: 460,
  marginLeft: 110,
  marginTop: 45,
  marginBottom: 60,
  style: {fontSize: "18px"},
  y: {
    type: "log", label: "Infections per day", grid: true,
    domain: [logTicks[0], logTicks[logTicks.length - 1]],
    ticks: logTicks,
    tickFormat: (d) => d >= 1e6 ? d3.format(".1~s")(d) : d3.format(",")(d)
  },
  x: {label: "Day", labelAnchor: "center"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([10], {stroke: "#8a8f98", strokeDasharray: "4 4"}),
    Plot.line(renewal, {
      x: "day", y: "infections", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3.5
    })
  ]
})
```

::: {.attribution}
Constant $R$, a gamma-shaped generation interval with shape 4, ten
infections on day 0 seeded on the exponential curve. Interactive this
talk.
:::

## What keeps going wrong

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Short delays are over-represented early in an epidemic. The long
  ones have not happened yet
- Chained models pass on a point estimate. The interval at the end is
  too narrow
- Bespoke code for each outbreak. Slow to adapt when the data change
- "We sometimes published nonsensical estimates"

::: {.callout-note}
Half of the 105 Belgian COVID-19 models reviewed by Bagaforo et al.
2026 had no behaviour component.
:::
:::
